evidence.intree_statement: Class Dinatural := { ditransform {x} : F (x, x) ~> G (x, x); dinaturality {x y} (f : x ~{C}~> y) : fmap[G] (op f ⋆⋆⋆ id) ∘ @ditransform y ∘ fmap[F] (id ⋆⋆⋆ f) ≈ fmap[G] (id ⋆⋆⋆ f) ∘ @ditransform x ∘ fmap[F] (op f ⋆⋆⋆ id) }   (with F G : C^op ∏ C ⟶ D)

statement_record.book: For S,T : C^op × C → B, a dinatural transformation α : S ⇒ T assigns each object c an arrow α_c : S(c,c) → T(c,c) such that for every f : c → c' the hexagon commutes: T(1,f)∘α_c∘S(f,1) = T(f,1)∘α_{c'}∘S(1,f) (both sides S(c',c) → T(c,c')).
statement_record.intree: Class Dinatural over F G : C^op ∏ C ⟶ D with component ditransform{x} : F(x,x) ~> G(x,x) and law dinaturality: fmap[G](op f ⋆⋆⋆ id) ∘ α_y ∘ fmap[F](id ⋆⋆⋆ f) ≈ fmap[G](id ⋆⋆⋆ f) ∘ α_x ∘ fmap[F](op f ⋆⋆⋆ id), both sides F(y,x) ~> G(x,y).
statement_record.strength_comparison: same — the setoid-rephrased hexagon is exactly Mac Lane's dinaturality condition with variance made explicit (op f ⋆⋆⋆ id = the S(f,1)/T(f,1) contravariant action, id ⋆⋆⋆ f = the S(1,f)/T(1,f) covariant action); domain/codomain F(y,x) ~> G(x,y) matches S(c',c) → T(c,c') under c=x,c'=y. The file's own header and nLab citation confirm the correspondence. No extra hypotheses; no special-casing.

verifier.notes: Independently read Theory/Dinatural.v: the Dinatural class (line 51) with ditransform{x}:F(x,x)~>G(x,x) and the dinaturality hexagon (lines 56-58) is a faithful setoid rephrasing of Mac Lane's condition; I verified the variance/orientation by hand (library RHS = Mac Lane LHS, domain F(y,x)~>G(x,y) = S(c',c)→T(c,c')). Evidence quote is exact; strength 'same' is honest. File registered in _CoqProject. evidence.intree_statement: Program Instance Diagonal {C : Category} (J : Category) : C ⟶ [J, C] := { fobj := fun x => {| fobj := fun _ => x ; fmap := fun _ _ _ => id[x] |}; ... }  — the constant functor at x (every object ↦ x, every morphism ↦ id[x]); notation Δ(c) := Diagonal _ c. This is exactly Mac Lane's 'dummy in both variables = constant at b' case (Δ(b) : C^op ∏ C ⟶ B).

Program Instance Fst {C D : Category} : C ∏ D ⟶ C := { ... }; Program Instance Snd {C D : Category} : C ∏ D ⟶ D := { ... }  — the projection functors π₁,π₂, through which a one-variable functor may be precomposed to become 'dummy in a variable', but no named predicate captures this.

statement_record.book: A functor T : C^op × C → B is 'dummy' in a variable if it factors through the projection deleting that variable (essentially a one-variable functor); 'dummy in both variables' means it is constant at an object b (T(c,c')=b, T(f,f')=1_b).
statement_record.intree: The 'dummy in both variables' case is the constant/diagonal functor Δ(b) : (C^op ∏ C) ⟶ B (Functor/Diagonal.v). The projection functors Fst/Snd : C ∏ D ⟶ C, D exist (Construction/Product.v), so 'dummy in one variable' = F ∘ Snd (resp. F ∘ Fst) is expressible by composition, but is not defined or named as a predicate.
statement_record.strength_comparison: intree-weaker: only the both-variables-dummy case has a direct named in-tree counterpart (the constant functor Δ, which is actively used, e.g. as Δw in Structure/Wedge.v). The general 'dummy in one variable = factors through a projection' is expressible from primitives (Fst/Snd + composition) but is not formalized as a named concept, and the reduction of a one-variable functor to a bifunctor via a projection is nowhere developed.

gap: No in-tree predicate for a bifunctor being independent of (‘dummy’ in) one of its two arguments, i.e. factoring through π₁/π₂. Only the degenerate both-variables case (the constant functor Δ) is named and used; the one-variable-dummy framing that Mac Lane uses to exhibit ordinary/covariant–contravariant natural transformations as special dinatural transformations is not formalized.

evidence.intree_statement: Class Wedge `(F : C^op ∏ C ⟶ D) := { wedge_obj : D; wedge_map {x : C} : wedge_obj ~{D}~> F (x, x); ump_wedges {x y : C} (f : x ~{C}~> y) : bimap[F] id f ∘ wedge_map ≈ bimap[F] (op f) id ∘ wedge_map }  — a dinatural transformation from the constant Δw to F (Mac Lane's dual wedge β : b ⇒ T).
Definition Cowedge `(F : C^op ∏ C ⟶ D) := @Wedge (C^op) (D^op) (F^op).  — the dual: legs F(x,x) ~> d, i.e. Mac Lane's extranatural α : S ⇒ b (components S(c,c) → b).

statement_record.book: When T=b is constant, a dinatural α : S ⇒ b (α_c : S(c,c)→b with α_c∘S(f,1)=α_{c'}∘S(1,f), 'square 3') is an extranatural / supernatural transformation, or wedge, from S to b; dually a wedge β : b ⇒ T (β_c : b→T(c,c) with T(1,f)∘β_c=T(f,1)∘β_{c'}, 'square 4').
statement_record.intree: Wedge F: apex wedge_obj w with legs wedge_map : w ~> F(x,x) and condition bimap[F] id f ∘ wedge_map[x] ≈ bimap[F] (op f) id ≈ wedge_map[y] (i.e. F(1,f)∘β_x = F(f,1)∘β_y = Mac Lane square 4). Cowedge F = Wedge F^op captures the dual with legs F(x,x)~>d (Mac Lane square 3).
statement_record.strength_comparison: same — ump_wedges is exactly Mac Lane's square-4 wedge condition (bimap[F] id f = F(1,f), bimap[F] (op f) id = F(f,1); under x=c,y=c' this is T(1,f)∘β_c = T(f,1)∘β_{c'}), and Cowedge gives the square-3 (extranatural-to-constant) direction. Both directions of Mac Lane's def3 are present. Only the terminology differs: the library says 'wedge/cowedge' and does not use 'extranatural/supernatural', but the mathematical content is identical.
